name: Chafa
summary: A terminal image and media viewer whose CLI and C library decode media, map pixels to terminal symbols or graphics protocols, and emit terminal-specific output.

features.name: Media loader and frame pipeline
features.description: The fixed source separates public image/frame objects from CLI media loaders and a media pipeline that supports image formats, animation, and frame iteration before terminal rendering.
benefits: Keeps decoding and frame selection separate from terminal output
Allows the CLI to process still images and animated media through one pipeline
costs: Format and animation support adds loader and frame-lifetime complexity
Decoded media can require substantially more memory than terminal output

features.name: Pixel-to-symbol canvas model
features.description: Chafa exposes canvas, frame, placement, and symbol-map types. The rendering path reduces image data into terminal cells and symbols while retaining color, dithering, and placement configuration.
benefits: Provides a reusable library boundary above terminal escape sequences
Supports different symbol sets and color strategies for the same image
costs: Terminal-cell quantization loses information relative to a pixel display
Dithering, palette, and placement choices affect output quality and cost

features.name: Terminal capability and graphics backends
features.description: The source contains terminal databases and information objects plus dedicated kitty, iTerm2, and Sixel canvas implementations. Output is therefore selected against terminal capabilities rather than emitted through one universal encoding.
benefits: Uses richer graphics protocols when the terminal advertises support
Retains text and ANSI-oriented output paths for broader compatibility
costs: Capability detection and protocol-specific encoders widen the compatibility surface
Terminal behavior can differ from the capabilities reported by its environment

features.name: CLI batch and stream boundary
features.description: The chafa executable composes path queues, stream readers/writers, terminal handling, and media loading around the library canvas. This makes the product surface a bounded CLI pipeline rather than a resident image runtime.
benefits: Supports shell composition and bounded processing of multiple inputs
Keeps command-line orchestration outside the reusable rendering types
costs: Process lifetime and stream errors cross several independently configured stages
Interactive terminal behavior is difficult to reproduce in non-interactive automation

mathematical_views.question: How does a media frame become a terminal cell or graphics-protocol sequence?
assumptions: A decoded frame is an input image state
Canvas and symbol-map operations are rendering transformations
Terminal capability selection chooses an output encoding
The model abstracts codec implementation and terminal display behavior

mathematical_views.question: Which output backend is admissible for a terminal capability set and requested format?
assumptions: Capabilities are observations supplied by terminal information and environment configuration
Backend support is modeled as a compatibility relation, not a guarantee of visual equivalence
Kitty, iTerm2, Sixel, and text/ANSI paths are distinct output strategies

mathematical_views.question: How do input paths or streams transition through loading, frame processing, rendering, and terminal emission?
assumptions: Each input can produce zero or more frames
Queue and stream stages can fail independently
The model describes the CLI boundary and does not claim exact scheduling

benefits: Multiple media formats and frames share one processing boundary
costs: Loader and frame lifecycle complexity increases memory and error handling work

benefits: One image model can target several terminal presentations
costs: Cell resolution and palette constraints limit fidelity

benefits: Protocol-specific paths can use richer terminal graphics features
costs: Backend proliferation makes compatibility and testing broader

benefits: The CLI composes naturally with files, pipes, and shell workflows
costs: Terminal state and stream failures complicate deterministic automation
